title: Few supports for life
hook: every pill bottle lists side effects; Nagarjuna says even the few supports of life can turn against it
tomorrow: at the very end, what actually helps?

segments.voice: Yesterday, many causes of death: a life more fragile than a bubble in the wind, so waking up is a wonder. Fragile. Today, the other side of that scale.

Every pill bottle comes with a folded sheet of side effects in tiny print. Food has its own warnings: allergies, choking hazards, best before. So can the very things that keep you alive also hurt you? Nagarjuna said yes, plainly, in a second letter of advice to a king, and Buddhists have leaned different ways on what to do with it.
screen: `SIDE EFFECTS IN TINY PRINT.` → `WHAT KEEPS YOU ALIVE CAN HURT.` → `SO WHAT DO YOU DO?`

segments.voice: In his Precious Garland, Nagarjuna writes that the causes of death are many, the things that keep us alive are few, and even those can become causes of death. Food, medicine, shelter, warmth: the few supports. And the same food can choke; the same medicine can harm. So what do you do with a body like that? Buddhists have leaned two ways, and both have deep roots. The first view: care for it. In the traditional story of the Buddha's life, he nearly starved himself in harsh practice, then accepted a bowl of milk-rice from a young woman named Sujata, and with his strength back, sat down and woke up. The body is the boat you cross in; neglect it and there's no crossing. The second view: don't cling to it. The few supports will fail sooner or later, and if all your peace hangs on them, there's no peace. Hold the body like something borrowed. Here's a place the two meet. In the Majjhima Nikaya, monks learn a reflection for every meal and every medicine: I use this wisely, not for fun or for show, but to keep this body going, to ease pain and sickness, so the practice can go on. Care, fully. Cling, not at all. Few supports: tend them well, and don't lean your whole weight on them.
screen: `MANY CAUSES, FEW SUPPORTS.` · `CARE FOR THE BOAT.` · `DON'T CLING TO WHAT'S BORROWED.` · `USE IT WISELY, FOR THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `FEW SUPPORTS.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip and feel it all the way down: one of the few supports, arriving. If there isn't, take one full breath the same way. Then sit with the body that sip or breath just cared for, without needing it to last forever.
Few supports for life: food, medicine, shelter, warmth. Few, and fallible. Tend them wisely, without clinging.
Here's the line: few supports, tended well and held lightly, like something borrowed. Day sixteen thirty-four, cared for.

screen: `DAY 1634 COUNTS.` → `DEATH AND DYING · 9 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: AT THE END, WHAT ACTUALLY HELPS?`

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries monks and nuns recite reflections on the use of food, robes, lodging and medicine, often daily; lay Buddhists sometimes say a short meal reflection before eating.

fork.setup: your friend says the 'don't cling to the body' view is just an excuse to skip the gym and eat junk. what's that view's strongest case?

supports fail sooner or later; peace that hangs only on them breaks.

fork.reveal: not neglect: non-clinging. both views meet in the monks' reflection: use food and medicine wisely, care fully, cling not at all.

Nagarjuna.meaning: an Indian Buddhist philosopher of the Mahayana

Sujata.meaning: the young woman who, tradition says, gave the Buddha milk-rice

Majjhima Nikaya.meaning: the middle-length discourses of the Buddha in the Pali canon

sources.ref: Nagarjuna, Ratnavali (Precious Garland): the causes of death are many, those of life few, and even these can become causes of death
Majjhima Nikaya 2 (Sabbasava Sutta: the wise reflection on using almsfood and medicine)
traditional life story of the Buddha (Nidanakatha): Sujata's offering of milk-rice before the awakening
